Spatiotemporal HM forecasting · branch ensemble

Uncertainty by Construction

How a per-pixel forecast interval becomes a set of complete, spatially coherent maps — and how we check that the result is honest at every scale from one kilometre to a continent.

Written
2026-08-17

OrientationWhat problem the ensemble solves

For every pixel and horizon the model publishes three numbers: a central forecast, and a lower and upper bound forming a 95% interval. The model on main produces exactly this and stops there.

Per-pixel intervals answer “how uncertain is this one pixel?”. They cannot answer “how uncertain is this district, this ecoregion, this country?” — because to add uncertainty up you must know how the errors at different pixels relate to one another. Two convenient assumptions bracket the truth, and both are badly wrong:

  • Errors perfectly correlated — just average the bounds. Aggregate coverage went 0.98 → 1.00: the interval became so wide it was always right, and therefore useless.
  • Errors independent — add in quadrature. Coverage collapsed 0.284 → 0.045 → 0.009 as blocks grew. Independent errors cancel, so a large region looks almost perfectly known. It is not.

The truth sits in between, and exactly where depends on the real spatial correlation of the model’s errors. The ensemble exists to represent that correlation explicitly.

An ensemble is M complete maps — “members”. Each is one plausible version of the world consistent with the published bounds. To get uncertainty at any scale you compute your quantity on every member and look at the spread. Aggregation stops being a modelling assumption and becomes arithmetic.

Section 1Central and quantile models

The trunk is a 4-layer ConvLSTM over three input timesteps (t−10, t−5, t), hidden dimension 64, 3×3 kernels, feeding twelve independent heads — four horizons × {lower, central, upper}. Inputs are HM and its component layers, seven static rasters, and eight learned location-encoder channels. That much is shared with main.

What changed

The central head predicts change, not level

On main the head predicts absolute HM, so it must first reproduce HM at t₀ through the trunk before adding anything. That reproduction is not free. On the 53–70% of pixels whose true change is under 0.001 — where the right answer is “emit t₀ unchanged” — the model still emitted change with sd ≈ 0.0075 HM, larger than the entire signal being predicted. With a skip connection and a zero-initialised output convolution the model starts at exact persistence and “nothing happens” is free to say. This was the large effect.

A long-range covariate the trunk cannot see

The trunk’s receptive radius is about 10 px, set by its 3×3 kernels. So it cannot see whether change happened 30–100 px away — which is the single best predictor of whether change is possible at all. Beyond 100 px from past change, not one of 493,240 measured pixels moved by more than 0.01 in twenty years.

We precompute, on the full raster, the distance from every pixel to the nearest pixel that changed by >0.01 in the previous decade, and hand both head families eight channels derived from it: occupancy within 1 / 3 / 10 / 30 / 100 px, log1p(distance)/10, the signed past change, and HM at t₀.

why it must be precomputed globally

Derived inside a 128 px training chip, every radius ≥ 30 px saturates into “is there any change anywhere in this chip” — measured at 0.752 mean occupancy for a single past-change pixel. That is an artifact of framing, not geography.

The interval is built around the central forecast

On main the three heads predict independently, so nothing stops the +10 yr interval being narrower than the +5 yr one. It was: the h=10 half-width was smaller than h=5’s while the error it had to cover was 1.5× larger, and coverage there fell to 0.892. Now each quantile head emits a non-negative half-width increment that accumulates across horizons around the (detached) central forecast. Spread cannot shrink with lead time, and lower ≤ central ≤ upper is structural rather than clipped afterwards.

A data-loader bug, fixed

Grid-mode sampling ignored the split mask entirely, so validation and test metrics were computed over the whole globe instead of held-out geography. Any val_coverage_* number from before that fix is not comparable to one after it.

Skill vs persistence compares the model against the forecast “nothing will change”. Negative means you would do better predicting no change at all. On main the model lost to persistence at +5 and +10 years — its squared error at +5 yr was 2.2× worse than doing nothing. It now wins at every horizon, and by more at longer lead, which is the sensible ordering. Scorecard on southern Africa: 73/137 → 101/127; the same chain scores 111/133 on Africa.

Latent defects found while auditing

None of these degrade the model. They are wasted work, or hazards for whoever reads the numbers next.

The histogram loss has never trained anything

compute_histogram bins by boolean comparison and sums into a plain torch.zeros buffer, so the loss carries no gradient at all — verified: requires_grad=False, and backward() raises. It has sat in the central objective at weight 1.0 for the whole project without moving a parameter.

It is not harmless: it is inside val_total_loss, which ModelCheckpoint selects on, and it swings ~60× between adjacent epochs. Making it differentiable was tried and is worse — h=20 RMSE +6.4% — because its rarity weights favour rare large-change bins ~240×, chasing the marginal distribution of change at the expense of the conditional mean.

  • The four horizons are trained 4 : 3 : 2 : 1. end_year is sampled from (2000, 2005, 2010, 2015) and targets past 2020 are NaN-masked, so h=20 gets a target from one window only. Validation uses fixed years and is balanced, so nothing in val_* reveals this.
  • The model saturates by about epoch 5. Neither the training nor the validation curve trends afterwards; tripling the budget to 450 epochs changes nothing measurable. Epoch 17 and epoch 75 give the same regional error. So the 150-epoch schedule is mostly sampling noise and save_top_k=1 picks the luckiest draw — on 34 validation chips.
  • Training is not deterministic at a fixed seed. Two runs with identical flags and --seed 42 differ in 54 of 62 tensors after three epochs. Any “is this change inert?” check must be distributional, never bit-exact.

Issues that bear on validity

Read this before comparing configurations

Run-to-run variance exceeds every effect measured since the central-field change. Two k=5 trainings of one configuration — five folds, 4.36 M pixels, identical pipeline — differ by 7 scorecard rows out of 128. Twenty-two model experiments were run in a dedicated phase and none produced an effect larger than that band, which is why none was adopted. The large historical gains (+18 and +11 rows) clear it comfortably and stand. But any future comparison inside ±7 rows needs replicate training runs to mean anything.

  • Every h=20 number is in-sample in time. Only the window ending 2000 reaches +20 yr inside the observed record. That horizon is validated on held-out geography but never on held-out time — and it is the one that matters most for a 2040 forecast.
  • Southern-Africa findings are provisional. It changes 2–4× less than Africa at every HM level, and its near-pristine stratum is 6% of the region against 40% of Africa. Measured: the interval-width error the post-hoc layer exists to correct is roughly twice as large on southern Africa as on Africa.
  • There is no production model, and one cannot be validated directly. See §4.

Section 2Ensembles

Everything in this section is new on this branch. main has none of it.

Two requirements, two separable steps

We want M maps, each satisfying two things at once:

  1. At each pixel, the right distribution. If the model says a pixel is 0.30 with a 95% interval of [0.25, 0.42], then across members that pixel should average 0.30, fall below 0.25 about 2.5% of the time and above 0.42 about 2.5% of the time. This is the marginal.
  2. Neighbouring pixels wrong together. Real errors are organised: if the model under-predicts a city’s expansion it does so across the whole city, not at every second pixel. This is the spatial correlation.

The tool that delivers both is a copula — which, stripped of the name, is a two-step recipe:

An analogy: think of z as a map of “how unlucky is this pixel today”, drawn so that nearby places have similar luck. Step B translates each pixel’s luck into an HM value using that pixel’s own uncertainty. Same luck map, different pixels, different outcomes.

The marginal — what distribution sits at each pixel

The simplest choice honouring the published triple is a median-spliced two-piece normal: a normal with one standard deviation below the median and another above, chosen so the 2.5th percentile lands exactly on the lower bound, the median exactly on the central forecast, and the 97.5th exactly on the upper. Closed-form and exact.

Its weakness is shape. Measured in units of the published half-width, the real error is far more concentrated in the middle and far heavier in the far tail than any normal:

P(|e|>0.25)P(|e|>0.5)P(|e|>1)kurtosis
Gaussian — what the two-piece assumes0.8030.6170.3173
observed, +5 yr0.3420.1940.08820 366
observed, +20 yr0.4920.2540.082928

So we replace the shape while keeping the three anchor points exact: the residual’s own quantile function is fitted on a 512-knot grid and normalised so that u = 0.025 / 0.5 / 0.975 still map precisely to lower / central / upper.

A structural limit worth stating plainly

Because the shape normalises each side by that side’s own 2.5/97.5 quantile — exactly what makes the bounds exact — the fitted marginal is the residual’s distribution stretched to fill the published interval. Measured stretch at +20 yr: 1.3–3.3× up, 1.3–7.1× down. So any marginal preserving the published bounds necessarily re-injects whatever width error those bounds carry. No shape can fix a width problem — which is why per-class half-width factors exist as a separate step, and why the post-hoc lever is considered exhausted.

The spatial field, from scratch

This is the part that makes members look like maps rather than static.

Why you cannot just add noise

Draw an independent value at every pixel and the map looks like television static — and every aggregate comes out far too certain, because independent errors cancel when you average them. Real error maps have patches. Getting the patch structure right is the problem.

Describing the structure: spectrum, not variogram

Two standard descriptions of how a field varies with distance. A variogram is the average squared difference between pairs of pixels a given distance apart. A power spectrum says how much of the field’s variance sits at each spatial frequency — low frequency meaning big smooth blobs, high frequency meaning fine speckle.

We fit the spectrum, and that was a deliberate correction. A variogram is evaluated at lags, where two long-range components can absorb the fit while leaving the middle empty. Measured against the real residual, the variogram-fitted mixture carried 4.9× too much power beyond 50 px and only 0.47× what it should at 3–10 px — the band holding 47% of the observed variance. Visually: smooth blobs where the truth is structured speckle. Fitting the radial spectrum brings those to 0.94× and 0.88×.

Why the longest range is added by hand

A power spectrum computed from a mean-subtracted field is blind to frequency zero — the overall level. But frequency zero is precisely what controls whether a whole region’s average is uncertain. Fit the spectrum alone and every large aggregate comes out overconfident. So a long-range component (1500 px) is added at weight 0.40, calibrated from aggregate error rather than from the spectrum. Swept 0.15–0.70 it moves essentially one thing — the spread-skill ratio, 0.82 → 1.52, monotonically — so it is identifiable from that metric alone.

The kernel: Matérn, not Gaussian

The correlation function’s shape matters as much as its range. A Gaussian kernel produces infinitely smooth fields — soft blobs. Real error fields have rough, textured edges. The Matérn family has a smoothness parameter ν; at ν = 0.5 it is the exponential kernel, rough at short range. Swept over 0.5–1.5, ν = 0.5 fits best.

Building the field affordably: circulant embedding

Generating a correlated field naively means factorising an N×N covariance matrix where N is the pixel count — impossible at 63 million pixels. Circulant embedding sidesteps it using one fact from Fourier analysis: if a field’s correlation depends only on the separation between points, then in frequency space the different frequencies are independent.

Coupling the four horizons

The horizons must not be independent. A member showing a city expanding fast by 2005 should still show it expanding by 2020. The normal-score fields are chained by an AR(1) process, z(h) = ρ·z(h−1) + √(1−ρ²)·ε(h), with ρ estimated from the residuals’ own between-horizon correlation. This keeps each field marginally standard normal while making consecutive horizons correlated.

The two guarantees, and how members are stored

Two properties hold by construction and are asserted as hard gates: the ensemble’s median equals the published central forecast, and its 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles equal the published bounds. That is what makes the ensemble a representation of the published product rather than a second, competing one. Whatever the ensemble says, the headline maps are unchanged.

Members are stored as int16 at scale 1/32767 — lossless to about 3×10⁻⁵, far below any quantity of interest — and every member’s random seed is recorded, so any ensemble regenerates exactly and a superseded one can be deleted and rebuilt in about three minutes.

Section 3The scorecard

Eight families of targets, scored per (target × horizon × scale), each failure carrying a diagnosis of which knob would move it. Africa, k=5, M=400, the shipped configuration: 111 of 133 scoreable rows pass. The same chain on southern Africa reads 101/127. Fourteen targets are reported but not gated.

The two regions are not interchangeable, and the differences run both ways. Africa has 158 ecoregions against southern Africa’s 18, which turns several aggregate targets from statistically undecidable into real tests; it also has enough remote country to populate the far distance bands, exposing a failure the smaller extent cannot see. Compare families, never totals.

T1Is each pixel’s uncertainty right? Does the truth fall inside the 95% interval 95% of the time — overall, and within each class of pixel? Pooled coverage is 0.938–0.944, mildly under at every horizon, where southern Africa was mildly over: about half the width machinery was compensating for that region’s own error structure. The class version is the one that matters — pooled coverage of 0.966 once coexisted with 0.335 in the high-change class.29 / 33
T2Is uncertainty right at larger scales? Aggregate over 1 km, 10 km and 100 km blocks and over real ecoregions. Block coverage is 12/12 — the motivating problem of the project, solved, and now on a continent. The ecoregion family goes 3/8 → 7/8 because it was a resolution problem: with 18 units coverage can only take values k/18, so 18/18 = 1.000 fails a ±0.05 target while 17/18 = 0.944 passes. At 158 units the values are 0.981–0.994 and T2.4 passes for the first time. T2.5 is the mirror image — a rank test that gained power and now fails 2005 at p = 1.2e-6.37 / 41
T3Do members look like real maps? The one family that does not move between regions — 3/6 on both, T3.2 at 0.031 against 0.021. The correlation structure is the live defect and it is regionally invariant, which makes it the one thing southern-Africa iteration was not flattering. T3.2’s 30% target conflicts with T3.4: 86% of the residual’s variance is already decorrelated at the distance T3.2 scores, so passing it would mean generating a field smoother than reality.3 / 6
T4Are the horizons coherent? Spread non-decreasing in lead time sits at 0.712 against a ≥0.99 gate, markedly worse than southern Africa’s 0.937 — the one real cost of raising the marginal’s tail bound. Between-horizon correlation is reported only: no AR(1) target file exists for this configuration, so ρ fell back to 0.9.0 / 1
T5Hard gates — is the ensemble faithful to the published product? Median = central, percentiles = bounds, mask = mask. Non-negotiable. The member count is visible here: at M=100 the same ensemble scored T5.1 2/4, at M=400 it is 3/4 with h=20 missing by 0.0015. Nothing changed but the number of draws.11 / 12
T6Is the amount and sign of change realistic? Change quantiles are 7/8 against southern Africa’s 3/8, with ratios of 1.01–1.86 against 1.11–5.41 — the clearest place Africa is genuinely better. Large decreases and tail asymmetry are right. Small decreases are still over-produced 2.5–4.5×, and mostly not fixable by any per-pixel marginal: the ideal calculation still over-predicts 3.05×.19 / 24
T7Are members diverse but not absurd? Diversity passes at 0.256 mean pairwise correlation. Spread-skill sits at 1.891 against 1.0 ± 0.25 — over-spread, and worse than southern Africa’s 1.583. The remedy is known and undesirable, so it is recorded as a near-miss.1 / 2
T8Is change put in the right places? The remote band still receives essentially no invented change (1.4e-06 against a ≤0.002 allowance) — the clearest single improvement in the project, against 3% under the original heads. But Africa exposes the opposite error on the same axis: with real far-field observations to compare against, the ensemble produces far too many decreases out there (7.8× and 123×) and too few increases (0.107×). Southern Africa passes these rows only because its remote observed change is exactly zero.11 / 14
How to read it honestly

Read rows, not the total. Two settings once tied on count while one had quietly pushed near-nominal rows below target.

Member count is part of the measurement. Tolerances tighten as 1/√M, so comparisons must be at matched M. An M=100 comparison between two marginal families once reversed at M=400; the same 101/127 reads 99/127 at M=800.

Region is part of the measurement too, and not only through difficulty. Several aggregate targets are limited by the number of aggregation units rather than by the field. At 18 ecoregions a ±0.05 coverage target is undecidable and rows can fail on quantisation alone.

A single scorecard carries ±7 rows of run-to-run noise. Differences smaller than that are not interpretable without replicate training runs.

Section 4Evaluation and forecasting

How hindcasts are made honest

A hindcast is a forecast for a date that has already happened, so it can be checked. But a model must not be scored on data it trained on, and HM only exists from 1990 to 2020. The solution is five-fold cross-validation over geography: five models, each excluding one spatial fold from training, each predicting only the fold it never saw, stitched into one raster.

The seam that creates, and the recipe for it

Holding geography out has a visible consequence. The fold mask is a 128 px checkerboard — each chip is assigned independently — so adjacent tiles of the stitched map come from different models, joined with no blending. Wherever those models disagree, the join shows.

They disagree on one head only. On Africa at +20 yr, mean pairwise |foldi − foldj| is 0.0053 for the central field and 0.0040 for the lower bound, against 0.0383 for the upper. The step across a fold boundary is 1.08× the step inside a fold for central and lower and 2.01× for the upper — 47× the local background in quiet country, where nothing else is happening. A single fold model’s own large-area prediction is seamless at every period from 64 to 1024 px, so neither the ConvLSTM nor the overlap blending is involved: it is purely the mosaic.

The recipe, deliberately split in two

Products and display rasters are stitched as the fold mean — every fold averaged at every pixel. No mosaic, no seam: the upper bound’s fold-boundary ratio goes 31.9× → 1.9× after recalibration and an ensemble member 2.5× → 1.1×. This mixes in-sample and out-of-sample predictions by construction.

Everything scored stays on the holdout mosaic. A fold-mean raster is in-sample at every pixel and would score flatteringly.

The forward 2025–2040 forecast has no seam at all: nothing is held out, so no mosaic is built.

What was considered and not adopted

Repeated k-fold CV — each chip predicted out-of-fold R times from models trained on different subsets, then averaged — reduces the seam by √R. At R=5 the upper bound goes from 2.01× to about 1.45× and quiet country from 47× to ~21×. It does not remove it, it costs 5× the training budget, and it changes what is being scored: an average of R out-of-fold predictions has lower error than any single model, so unless the average is also what ships, the hindcast becomes optimistic in a way that does not transfer. Repeated seeds at a fixed fold mask is cheaper to reason about and still strictly out of sample, but averages only the training-noise component and delivers 1.24–1.76× at R=5.

To choose between them, fold 1 was retrained twice with only the seed changed. On the upper half-width the seed-to-seed spread is 0.0308 against a fold-to-fold 0.0335 at h=20; in variance terms training noise is 85% of the disagreement at h=20 and 44–63% at shorter horizons. Both schemes are therefore largely averaging away optimisation noise rather than genuine model diversity — which points at the training recipe as the cheaper lever. Switching the checkpoint monitor to val_central_loss alone already cuts the fold-to-fold upper-width spread from 0.0335 to 0.0275, an 18% reduction at no cost.

Coarser fold blocks (contiguous 1280 px fold territories instead of a 128 px checkerboard) are implemented but not trained. They cut seam density about 12×, so a typical viewing window sits inside one fold, though the step at the remaining seams is unchanged. The real argument is not cosmetic: the residual field’s fitted practical range is 99–166 px, typically ~130, against a 128 px fold tile — the current split holds geography out at one correlation length, so held-out skill is optimistic. Adopting it means retraining all five folds and makes every existing scorecard non-comparable.

The evaluation loop re-derives everything downstream of the model from that model’s own residuals — the recalibration, spectrum, AR(1) coupling, width factors and marginal shape. Carrying any of them over scores a new central field through an old model’s error structure, which is the single most productive source of convincing wrong numbers in this project.

Two diagnostics carry particular weight beyond the scorecard. The per-member test asks, for each member separately, where the observation ranks among the members — because a pool that is uniformly too hot still overlaps the truth, so pooling answers a weaker question than it appears to. And a closed-form predictor computes the member mean of P(Δ > threshold) analytically in 30 seconds, sharing no code with the GPU sampler — so agreement is evidence and disagreement localises a bug to the generation path.

The production gap

The state of play

Every checkpoint carrying these improvements was trained with a fold held out. No production model exists in this configuration. The only artifact that has ever made global forward predictions carries the old central head — the configuration measured at skill −1.23 at +5 yr, i.e. losing to “nothing will change”. Applying the new ensemble statistics to those old predictions would be exactly the error the loop is designed to prevent.

The forward path, once a production model exists: train with the same flags and no fold exclusion (chips are sampled globally either way, so this is the same model in every respect except that it uses all the geography); predict with inputs 2010 / 2015 / 2020 → targets 2025 / 2030 / 2035 / 2040, which is the identical +5/+10/+15/+20 structure so the residual statistics transfer directly; apply those statistics to the forward bounds; generate the forward ensemble with the same spectrum, shape and coupling.
